title: Signature Lineage-Aware Router
description: Signature edition: routing decisions consult each model's Signature lineage — training provenance, audit history, known failure modes — alongside capability. A model with the right skill but a tainted lineage is deprioritized automatically. This is a Signature original method.
method: Registry entries carry lineage stamps and audit flags; the router's score includes a lineage-trust term; tainted models require explicit override.
usage: Stamp every fine-tune with lineage; audit flags propagate to routing automatically.

demo.code:
models = [('sql-1b', 0.91, 'clean'), ('sql-1b-x', 0.93, 'tainted')]
ranked = sorted(models, key=lambda m: m[1] * (1.0 if m[2]=='clean' else 0.5), reverse=True)
print('lineage-aware ranking:', [m[0] for m in ranked])

title: Signature Cascading model escalation
description: Signature edition: Try the cheapest model first; only escalate to bigger models when the small one is uncertain. Cascades capture the easy 80% of traffic on tiny models and reserve the expensive flagship for genuinely hard queries — the standard cost/latency optimization for production LLM serving.
method: Run the small model; score its confidence (self-rating or a verifier); if below threshold, escalate with the small model's draft as context for the bigger model.
usage: Tune the threshold on labeled data: too low wastes money, too high hurts quality on the escalated slice.

demo.code:
conf = 0.42
print(f'small model confidence {conf}')
print('-> ESCALATE to medium model' if conf < 0.7 else '-> accept small model answer')

title: Signature Quality-verified routing feedback loop
description: Signature edition: The router isn't static: every routed request's outcome (user thumbs-up, task success, verifier score) feeds back to update routing weights. Models that deliver get more traffic; models that disappoint get less. Routing becomes a learning system, not a config file.
method: Log (query features, chosen model, outcome); periodically recompute per-model success rates by intent; update routing weights; A/B test weight changes.
usage: Define the outcome signal first (what counts as success); update weights on a schedule, not per request.

title: Signature Cost-aware routing with budgets
description: Signature edition: Every request carries a cost budget; the router picks the best model that fits. Interactive chat gets the cheap fast model, batch analytics gets the strong expensive one, and per-team budgets are enforced automatically. Cost becomes a first-class routing input, not an afterthought.
method: Estimate tokens, compute cost per candidate model, filter to those within budget, and pick the highest expected quality among them.
usage: Set budgets per use case; alert when the router consistently can't afford adequate quality (budget too tight, not router's fault).

demo.code:
budget, cands = 0.02, [('tiny', 0.002, 0.7), ('mid', 0.02, 0.85), ('max', 0.2, 0.95)]
fit = [c for c in cands if c[1] <= budget]
best = max(fit, key=lambda c: c[2])
print(f'budget ${budget}: candidates fit {len(fit)} -> choose {best[0]} (quality {best[2]})')

title: Signature Multi-signal ensemble routing
description: Signature edition: Instead of one signal, the router combines several — intent match, predicted difficulty, cost budget, latency deadline, and current load — into a single score per candidate model. Ensemble routing handles real production constraints where no single signal tells the whole story.
method: Score = w1*intent_match + w2*quality_fit + w3*cost_fit + w4*latency_fit - w5*load_penalty; pick argmax; weights tuned on historical outcomes.
usage: Start with hand-set weights, then tune on logged outcomes; expose the score breakdown for debugging.

demo.code:
cands = {'tiny': 0.72, 'mid': 0.81, 'max': 0.65}  # ensemble scores
best = max(cands, key=cands.get)
print('ensemble scores:', cands, '-> route to', best)

title: Signature Specialist fine-tune registry
description: Signature edition: The foundation of routing: a registry of fine-tuned micro-models, each with measured capability cards, eval scores, cost, and latency. Routers consult the registry; model ops updates it on every new fine-tune. Without the registry, routing is guesswork.
method: Register each model with (capabilities, eval scores, $/1k tokens, p99 latency); version entries; routers query by capability tags.
usage: Re-eval on every fine-tune; retire registry entries for deprecated models; make the registry the single source of truth.

demo.code:
registry = [{'name': 'sql-1b', 'tags': ['sql'], 'eval': 0.91, 'cost': 0.001}]
print('registry entry:', registry[0])
print('router query tags=[sql] -> sql-1b (eval 0.91)')

title: Signature Embedding nearest-specialist routing
description: Signature edition: Each specialist model is described by an embedding of its capability card ('expert in SQL tuning'); the query embedding is compared against all cards and the nearest specialist wins. Adding a new specialist is just adding a card — no router retraining needed.
method: Embed capability cards once; embed each query; cosine similarity picks the specialist; threshold below which the generalist handles it.
usage: Write honest capability cards (measured strengths, not marketing); re-embed cards when a model is fine-tuned.

demo.code:
cards = {'sql-1b': 'expert in SQL tuning', 'py-1b': 'expert in Python debugging'}
q = 'slow query'
best = max(cards, key=lambda k: sum(w in cards[k] for w in q.split()))
print(f'query {q!r} -> nearest specialist: {best}')

title: Signature Mixture-of-experts token routing
description: Signature edition: Inside MoE models (Mixtral, Switch Transformer), a learned router sends each token to 1-2 of many expert feed-forward networks. Total parameters are huge but active parameters per token stay small — the model equivalent of calling in only the specialists each word needs.
method: A gating network scores experts per token; top-k experts process the token; outputs combine weighted by gate scores; load-balancing loss keeps experts evenly used.
usage: Monitor expert utilization in production; collapsed routing (one expert does everything) means the MoE isn't earning its parameters.

demo.code:
import random
random.seed(1)
experts = [f'e{i}' for i in range(8)]
token, chosen = 'photosynthesis', sorted(random.sample(experts, 2))
print(f'token {token!r} routed to experts {chosen} (2 of 8 active)')

title: Signature Task-difficulty predictor routing
description: Signature edition: A tiny model predicts how hard a query is before any big model runs, and the router picks model size from the difficulty score. Easy lookups go to the 1B model; multi-hop reasoning goes to the 70B. Predicting difficulty up front avoids both under- and over-provisioning.
method: Train a difficulty regressor on (query features -> best model size) from historical quality data; route by predicted difficulty band.
usage: Retrain the predictor as models change; log mismatches where the chosen model failed.

demo.code:
difficulty = 0.82  # predicted
band = 'hard' if difficulty > 0.66 else 'medium' if difficulty > 0.33 else 'easy'
print(f'difficulty {difficulty} -> band {band} -> route to 70B model')
